events.text: Poole comes to Utterson's house at night and says something is wrong.
events.quote: he was surprised to receive a visit from Poole

events.text: Poole says the doctor has shut himself in the cabinet and he is afraid.
events.quote: he’s shut up again in the cabinet; and I don’t like it, sir

events.text: Poole says he thinks there has been foul play.
events.quote: “I think there’s been foul play,” said Poole, hoarsely.

events.text: Utterson rises, takes hat and greatcoat, and follows Poole.
events.quote: Mr. Utterson’s only answer was to rise and get his hat and greatcoat

events.text: They walk through the cold deserted London streets to the house.
events.quote: It was a wild, cold, seasonable night of March

events.text: They enter the hall where all the servants are huddled in fear.
events.quote: about the hearth the whole of the servants, men and women, stood huddled together like a flock of sheep

events.text: The housemaid whimpers and the maid weeps loudly.
events.quote: only the maid lifted her voice and now wept loudly

events.text: Poole orders the knife-boy to bring a candle.
events.quote: addressing the knife-boy, “reach me a candle

events.text: Poole leads Utterson to the laboratory and tells him to listen quietly.
events.quote: followed the butler into the laboratory building through the surgical theatre

events.text: Poole knocks and calls that Utterson asks to see him.
events.quote: “Mr. Utterson, sir, asking to see you,” he called

events.text: The voice inside complains that it cannot see anyone.
events.quote: “Tell him I cannot see anyone,” it said complainingly.

events.text: Poole asks whether that was his master's voice; Utterson says it seems much changed.
Poole declares his master was made away with eight days ago.
events.quote: master’s made away with; he was made away with eight days ago

events.text: Utterson calls the tale wild and argues a murderer would not stay.
events.quote: That is a very strange tale, Poole; this is rather a wild tale my man

events.text: Poole tells of a week of notes demanding a pure drug from chemists.
events.quote: him, or it, whatever it is that lives in that cabinet, has been crying night and day for some sort of medicine

events.text: Poole hands Utterson a crumpled note from Dr. Jekyll to Messrs. Maw.
events.quote: Poole felt in his pocket and handed out a crumpled note

events.text: Utterson notes the handwriting is the doctor's; Poole says he has seen him.

relation_context.story_before_this_passage:
During a Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield stop at a sinister door. Enfield recalls how a man trampled a girl, then paid her family £100 with a cheque that proved genuine. Enfield names him Hyde, deformed and detestable, still holding the key. Utterson says he knows the other party’s name. They agree never to speak of it again.

Utterson returns home troubled and studies Jekyll’s will, which leaves everything to Edward Hyde if Jekyll vanishes. He calls it madness and fears disgrace. At Cavendish Square, Lanyon says Jekyll grew too fanciful years ago and has never heard of Hyde. Unable to sleep, Utterson resolves to hunt Hyde. Keeping watch by the by-street door, he accosts a small man with a key, who admits Jekyll is out, gives his Soho address, then snarls and disappears inside. At Jekyll’s house, Poole confirms Hyde has a key, comes by the dissecting room, and all servants must obey him. Utterson goes home fearing Jekyll is in deep waters.

After dinner, Utterson stays behind with Dr. Jekyll and raises the will. Jekyll calls Lanyon a hide-bound pedant. When Utterson mentions young Hyde, Jekyll pales and refuses to hear more. Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll says he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses, yet takes great interest in him. Jekyll asks Utterson to help Hyde for his sake when he is gone. Utterson promises to bear with Hyde and get his rights.

[P10] “You stay too much indoors,” said the lawyer. “You should be out, whipping up the circulation like Mr. Enfield and me. (This is my cousin—Mr. Enfield—Dr. Jekyll.) Come now; get your hat and take a quick turn with us.”
[P11] “You are very good,” sighed the other. “I should like to very much; but no, no, no, it is quite impossible; I dare not. But indeed, Utterson, I am very glad to see you; this is really a great pleasure; I would ask you and Mr. Enfield up, but the place is really not fit.”
[P12] “Why, then,” said the lawyer, good-naturedly, “the best thing we can do is to stay down here and speak with you from where we are.”
[P13] “That is just what I was about to venture to propose,” returned the doctor with a smile. But the words were hardly uttered, before the smile was struck out of his face and succeeded by an expression of such abject terror and despair, as froze the very blood of the two gentlemen below. They saw it but for a glimpse for the window was instantly thrust down; but that glimpse had been sufficient, and they turned and left the court without a word. In silence, too, they traversed the by-street; and it was not until they had come into a neighbouring thoroughfare, where even upon a Sunday there were still some stirrings of life, that Mr. Utterson at last turned and looked at his companion. They were both pale; and there was an answering horror in their eyes.
[P14] “God forgive us, God forgive us,” said Mr. Utterson.
[P15] But Mr. Enfield only nodded his head very seriously, and walked on once more in silence.

known_before.bio: G. J. Utterson is a lawyer, a kinsman and friend of Richard Enfield, and an old friend of both Dr. Jekyll and Dr. Lanyon. He is a man of blameless past who is troubled by old sins. After Enfield told him of a faceless figure at a by-street door, he lay awake haunted, kept watch by that door, and resolved to hunt for Hyde. known_before.tagline: Elderly servant at Dr. Jekyll's house
known_before.bio: Poole is the elderly servant at Dr. Jekyll's house, obedient to his master and to Hyde as his superior. He told Utterson that Jekyll had gone out, confirmed Hyde had a key and came by the dissecting room door, said all servants had orders to obey Hyde, and that Hyde never dined there and mostly used the laboratory. He admitted Utterson to Jekyll's cabinet and told him no letter came except by post. He reported that Jekyll had shut his door against Utterson and was confined.
